public_rationale: The NANDA report's January–June 2025 research documents users recognizing unmet needs for memory, adaptation and workflow fit, supporting the claim about recognized limitations [e1]. But the categorical claim that the products do not perform their intended functions is too broad: users described ChatGPT as useful for brainstorming and first drafts [e1]. Enterprise users also praised general-purpose assistants such as ChatGPT and Copilot for flexibility and immediate utility, while criticizing custom tools for poor workflow fit [e2].
limitations: The implementation figures come from interviews, with varying sample sizes and success definitions; they do not establish a representative failure rate across enterprise AI products [e2].
Reported usefulness of general-purpose assistants does not establish that task-specific tools meet their workflow requirements [e2].
The user accounts document recognition of limitations, but do not establish an increase in recognition over time [e1].

The report defines successful task-specific implementation through reported sustained productivity or financial impact. Missing that threshold does not by itself establish technical nonfunctionality [e2].

from_speaker: The products don't do what they're meant to do
our_interpretation: Read this as an observation about enterprise generative AI tools discussed in the cited NANDA report: difficulty delivering intended workflow functions, together with users recognizing those limitations.
Do not equate a lack of measured profit impact with complete technical nonfunctionality.
Use January–June 2025, the research period of the report directly discussed in the surrounding passage.
Read 'people are realizing it' as documented user recognition. A claim that recognition increased over time would additionally require longitudinal evidence.
criteria.support_condition: Enterprise evaluations document failures to meet intended workflow requirements, and users explicitly recognize those failures.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evaluations document useful delivery of intended functions and satisfied users within the same enterprise-use scope. Substantial evidence of both failures and useful delivery warrants a mixed assessment.

evidence.explanation: The report records users identifying missing adaptation, memory and workflow fit, including this complaint. Its broader findings document stalled enterprise implementations, supporting both practical limitations and user recognition during the January–June research period.

evidence.explanation: The same enterprise research reports positive experiences with general-purpose assistants used at work, as well as successful implementations elsewhere in the report. This contradicts an unqualified conclusion that the products fail to deliver useful functions.
